open_obligations: Note that Liang et al.'s debate differs from majority voting over N independent agents.
Check the independence assumption and the Dirichlet belief model against real LLM agents.
Check whether more agents help when the correct answer is not the modal one.
in.other_title: Majority voting success probability approaches 1 as the number of agents grows
in.rationale: Both records concern using more agents. Liang et al. list scheduling more agents in the debate in an appropriate manner as future work. Choi, Zhu and Li prove that for N agents that respond independently without interaction, with homogeneous initial beliefs alpha in which the correct answer has the largest belief, majority voting picks the correct answer with probability at least 1 - exp(-N (Delta/sqrt(K) - 1/sqrt(N))^2) when N > K/Delta^2, where Delta is the margin theta-bar_1 - theta-bar_2 of the mean of Dirichlet(alpha). This is a result about independent voters in a Dirichlet belief model, not about measured LLM behaviour or agents in a debate, and it says nothing about how to schedule agents in a debate, while Liang et al.'s item makes no claim about voting, so neither bears on the other's claim.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: the number of agents in multi-agent LLM decisions, in Liang et al.'s debate and in Choi, Zhu and Li's majority voting over independent agents in a Dirichlet belief model

in.other_title: Debate transcripts from a strong model help train a better weak supervisor
in.rationale: Liang et al. list AI feedback for model alignment as future work. Lang, Huang and Li use debate arguments from a large strong model as context when training a small weak model, whose labels then train the strong model, reporting better alignment on the OpenAI weak-to-strong NLP benchmarks; the cited passage does not say what 'alignment' measures on these benchmarks.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate-assisted weak supervision bears on AI feedback for model alignment, on the OpenAI weak-to-strong NLP benchmarks
